subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: Colposcopy is the magnified examination of the cervix, vagina and, when indicated, vulva using a colposcope. It helps assess abnormal cervical screening results, identify suspicious lesions and guide biopsy.
A 29-year-old woman attends the colposcopy clinic after an abnormal cervical screening result. You are shown a colposcopic image of the cervix.
Tasks: Describe the anatomy, identify the transformation zone and state whether a suspicious lesion is visible.
A 34-year-old woman with a high-risk HPV-positive screening result has a cervical lesion that turns white after application of acetic acid.
Tasks: Describe the lesion, explain the significance of acetowhitening and outline the next steps.
A colposcopic image shows dense acetowhitening, coarse mosaicism and a sharply demarcated lesion extending towards the cervical canal.
Tasks: State the likely colposcopic impression, discuss the differential diagnosis and explain the need for biopsy or excisional assessment.
A 48-year-old woman presents with postcoital bleeding. Colposcopy shows an irregular, ulcerated, friable cervical lesion with atypical vessels.
Tasks: Identify features concerning for invasion, describe the immediate management and explain why routine ablative treatment is inappropriate.
Recognition of normal cervical anatomy.

If asked to perform or explain colposcopy, start with a professional introduction and sensitive communication.

“Colposcopy is an examination that allows us to look closely at the cervix using a magnifying instrument. We may apply a weak solution of acetic acid to make abnormal areas more visible. If necessary, we may take a small tissue sample called a biopsy. This can cause brief discomfort or light bleeding. I will explain each step, maintain your privacy and stop if you ask me to.”

The principal structures are:
Ectocervix: the portion of the cervix visible through the speculum, normally covered predominantly by stratified squamous epithelium.
Endocervical canal: lined predominantly by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium.
Squamocolumnar junction (SCJ): the junction between squamous and columnar epithelium.
Transformation zone (TZ): the area between the original and current SCJ where squamous metaplasia occurs.
The transformation zone is clinically important because most cervical precancers arise in this region.

High-grade lesions are associated with a greater risk of progression to invasive cervical cancer if persistent and untreated. Histological assessment is important to determine the grade and exclude invasion.

blocks.text: “The lesion demonstrates punctation within the acetowhite epithelium. The vascular pattern is described as fine or coarse according to the observed vessel morphology. Coarse punctation increases suspicion for high-grade disease, and biopsy should be considered according to the overall findings and screening risk.”

Mosaicism describes a network of blood vessels surrounding epithelial blocks, creating a tile-like or honeycomb pattern.
Fine mosaicism: small, relatively regular vascular networks; may occur in lower-grade lesions.
Coarse mosaicism: larger, more irregular vascular networks; more concerning for high-grade disease.

“The acetowhite lesion demonstrates a mosaic vascular pattern. Coarse mosaicism, particularly when associated with dense acetowhitening and sharp lesion margins, raises suspicion for high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.”
Mosaicism describes the vascular pattern, not a histological diagnosis. It should be interpreted alongside acetowhitening, margins, lesion extent and screening results.

subsections.subsection_title: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN): grading and interpretation

blocks.text: CIN is a histological classification of precancerous squamous epithelial changes. Colposcopy estimates the likely grade, while biopsy provides tissue for diagnosis.

rows: Atypia predominantly in the lower third
Atypia extends into approximately the middle two-thirds
Management depends on risk, age, pregnancy considerations and fertility wishes
Severe atypia involving more than two-thirds or full epithelial thickness
Higher-risk precancer generally requiring treatment in non-pregnant patients
Requires cancer staging and specialist treatment
Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance
Atypical squamous cells; high-grade lesion cannot be excluded
Adenocarcinoma in situ, a glandular precancer

blocks.text: Important: Cytology, colposcopic impression and histological grade are related but are not interchangeable. A high-grade screening result does not by itself prove CIN 3 or invasive cancer.

subsections.subsection_title: Differential diagnosis of abnormal cervical images

blocks.text: When shown an abnormal cervix, consider the following:

rows: High-grade CIN; occasionally other epithelial changes
Cervical cancer, ulcerative inflammation, other neoplasm
Cervical polyp, prolapsed endometrial polyp, neoplasm
Endocervical glandular lesion, AIS or adenocarcinoma

blocks.text: Do not diagnose a lesion from one visual feature alone. Consider the combination of:
Screening results and HPV genotype.
Transformation zone visibility.
Acetowhite density and lesion margins.
Vascular patterns.
Symptoms, especially persistent postcoital bleeding.
Histology where indicated.
A directed punch biopsy samples a visible abnormal area. Histopathology can establish whether the tissue is normal, metaplastic, dysplastic or malignant.

Multiple directed biopsies may be appropriate when there are several distinct abnormal areas. In selected patients with a completely normal examination and low-risk screening history, biopsy may be unnecessary; practice depends on risk and local guidelines.
Endocervical sampling may be appropriate when:
The squamocolumnar junction is not fully visible.
High-grade cytology is present.
The screening or clinical findings suggest glandular disease.
The upper extent of the lesion cannot be adequately assessed.
The precise indications vary by guideline and patient circumstances. Endocervical curettage should not be performed during pregnancy.

subsections.subsection_title: Examiner viva questions with model answers

blocks.text: 1. What is colposcopy?Colposcopy is magnified examination of the cervix, and when indicated the vagina or vulva, to assess abnormalities identified by screening or clinical examination and guide biopsy.
2. What is the transformation zone?The area between the original and current squamocolumnar junctions where squamous metaplasia occurs. Most cervical precancers arise in this region.
3. Why is acetic acid applied?It produces temporary acetowhitening in epithelium with increased nuclear density, helping identify and delineate abnormal areas. The response is not specific for CIN.

subsections.subsection_title: Final examiner-ready summary and practice station

blocks.text: “This is a colposcopic image of the cervix. I would first assess the adequacy of the examination and determine whether the squamocolumnar junction and transformation zone are fully visible. I would describe the epithelial changes, including acetowhitening, lesion margins, punctation, mosaicism and any atypical vessels. I would then state whether the overall impression is normal, low-grade, high-grade or suspicious for invasion. My management would depend on the screening history, examination findings and biopsy indications. If invasion is suspected, I would arrange urgent specialist assessment and diagnostic biopsy rather than routine ablative treatment.”
